metadata.title: Formative Quiz - Seminar 02: Operators, Redirection, Filters, Loops

questions.question_text: Which operator executes the second command ONLY if the first one succeeds (exit code 0)?

feedback.correct:
The && operator (logical AND) executes the command on the right ONLY if the one on the left
returns exit code 0 (success). It is useful for chains of dependent commands.

incorrect.A: The ; operator always executes both commands, regardless of result
incorrect.C: The || operator executes the second command when the first one FAILS
incorrect.D: The & operator launches the command in background, does not check exit code

questions.question_text: What does the & operator do when placed at the end of a command?

options.text: Connects stdout to the stdin of another command

feedback.correct:
The & operator placed at the end of a command sends it to the background,
immediately freeing the terminal for other commands.

incorrect.A: Confusion with other operators

questions.question_text:
```bash
mkdir test && echo "Created" || echo "Error"
```
If the directory `test` ALREADY EXISTS, what is displayed?

feedback.correct:
mkdir fails (non-zero exit code) when the directory exists.
&& is not executed (echo "Created" skipped).
|| IS executed because the previous chain failed.
Result: "Error"

incorrect.A: Does not understand that mkdir returns error when the directory exists

questions.question_text:
```bash
ls /inexistent | wc -l
echo "Exit code: $?"
```
What will the displayed exit code be?

options.text: The exit code of ls (non-zero, error)
The exit code of wc (0, success)

incorrect.A: Believes the pipe transmits the first command's exit code

questions.question_text:
```bash
x=1
{ x=2; echo "In braces: $x"; }
echo "After braces: $x"

y=1
( y=2; echo "In parentheses: $y"; )
echo "After parentheses: $y"
```
What are the final values for x and y in the main shell?

feedback.correct:
{} executes in the CURRENT shell - modifications persist (x=2).
() executes in a SUBSHELL - modifications are lost (y remains 1).

incorrect.A: Does not understand that () creates a subshell

questions.question_text: Which operator appends text to the END of an existing file (without overwriting it)?

feedback.correct:
>> (append) adds to the end of the file.
> overwrites the file completely.
< redirects input.
2> redirects stderr.

incorrect.A: > overwrites the file

questions.question_text:
```bash
# Variant A:
ls /home /inexistent > out.txt 2>&1

# Variant B:
ls /home /inexistent 2>&1 > out.txt
```
Which variant sends BOTH (stdout and stderr) to out.txt?

feedback.correct:
Redirections are evaluated from left to right!

Variant A: 
1. > out.txt: stdout → out.txt
2. 2>&1: stderr → where stdout is NOW (out.txt)

Variant B:
1. 2>&1: stderr → where stdout is NOW (terminal)
2. > out.txt: stdout → out.txt (stderr remains on terminal!)

incorrect.B: Does not understand the evaluation order of redirections
incorrect.C: Believes the order does not matter
incorrect.D: Does not know the classic syntax, believes only &> works

questions.question_text:
```bash
ls /inexistent 2>/dev/null
echo $?
```
What value will $? (exit code) have?

options.text: Non-zero (error, because the directory does not exist)

feedback.correct:
2>/dev/null suppresses only the OUTPUT of the error, not the exit code!
The command still fails (non-zero exit code), we just do not see the message.

incorrect.A: COMMON: Believes that suppressing the message = success

questions.question_text: How do you save BOTH stdout AND stderr to a file log.txt using Bash?

feedback.correct:
&> is the Bash syntax for redirecting both streams.
Equivalent to: cmd > log.txt 2>&1

Option A/C can cause overwriting problems.
Option D (tee) does not capture stderr.

incorrect.A: Can cause concurrency problems during writing

questions.question_text:
```bash
echo -e "a\nb\na\nb" | uniq
```
What does this command display?

feedback.correct:
CLASSIC TRAP: uniq removes only CONSECUTIVE duplicates!
Input: a, b, a, b - none is consecutive with another identical one.
All remain.
Correct pattern: sort | uniq or sort -u

incorrect.A: 80% believe this! Do not know that uniq removes only CONSECUTIVE duplicates

questions.question_text:
```bash
echo "one two three" | cut -f2
```
What does it display?

feedback.correct:
cut -f uses TAB as the default delimiter, not space!
The string "one two three" does not contain TAB.
With no TAB found, it returns the entire line.
For spaces: cut -d' ' -f2

incorrect.A: Believes that cut splits by spaces by default

questions.question_text: Which command counts how many UNIQUE lines (without duplicates) a file contains?

feedback.correct:
sort | uniq removes all duplicates (by sorting first).
wc -l counts the resulting lines.

Option A counts ALL lines.
Option C does not sort, so uniq does not remove all duplicates.
Option D - wc does not have a -u flag.

incorrect.A: Counts all lines, including duplicates
incorrect.C: uniq without sort does not remove all duplicates

questions.question_text: How do you extract ONLY column 3 from a CSV file (comma separator)?

feedback.correct:
cut -d',' sets the delimiter to comma.
-f3 selects field 3.

Option A uses TAB by default (wrong for CSV).
Option C: awk by default uses spaces/tabs.
Option D: complicated and incorrect regex.

incorrect.A: cut by default uses TAB, not comma
incorrect.C: awk by default does not use comma as separator
incorrect.D: The regex does not correctly extract the column

questions.question_text: Which command displays the last 20 lines of a file?

feedback.correct:
tail -N displays the last N lines.
head -N displays the FIRST N lines.
cat -n numbers lines, does not limit them.
less -20 is not valid syntax for this purpose.

incorrect.A: head displays from the BEGINNING

questions.question_text:
```bash
echo "hello" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
```
What does it display?

feedback.correct:
tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' transforms ALL lowercase letters to uppercase.
Each character from the first set is replaced with its correspondent from the second.

incorrect.A: Does not understand the tr function

questions.question_text:
```bash
N=5
for i in {1..$N}; do
    echo $i
done
```
What does this script display?

feedback.correct:
TRAP: Brace expansion happens BEFORE variable expansion!
{1..$N} cannot be expanded because $N is not yet interpreted.
It remains literal: "{1..5}"
The loop iterates once with i="{1..5}"

Solutions: seq, for ((i=1; i<=N; i++))

incorrect.A: 70% believe this! Do not know the expansion order
incorrect.D: Believes the loop does not execute at all

questions.question_text:
```bash
count=0
echo -e "a\nb\nc" | while read line; do
    ((count++))
done
echo "Count: $count"
```
What does it display?

feedback.correct:
SUBSHELL PROBLEM: The right side of the pipe runs in a SUBSHELL!
Modifications to count are made in the subshell.
When the subshell ends, the modifications are LOST.
The main shell sees count=0.

Solution: while read line; do ... done < <(echo -e "a\nb\nc")

incorrect.A: 65% believe this! Do not know the subshell problem

questions.question_text:
```bash
for i in 1 2 3; do
    if [ $i -eq 2 ]; then
        break
    fi
    echo $i
done
echo "After loop"
```
What is displayed?

feedback.correct:
break exits only the loop, not the script!
At i=1: echo 1
At i=2: break (exit from loop before echo)
Continues with "After loop"

exit would have stopped the script completely.

questions.question_text: What is the CORRECT way to iterate through .txt files in the current directory?

feedback.correct:
for f in *.txt uses glob expansion which preserves complete names.

Option A: $(ls *.txt) splits incorrectly on spaces in names.
Option C: cat reads the CONTENT of files, not names.
Option D: invalid syntax for while.

incorrect.A: $(ls *.txt) causes problems with spaces in names
incorrect.C: cat reads content, not file names
incorrect.D: while does not have this syntax

questions.question_text: How do you read a file line by line in Bash?

options.text: while read line; do ... done < file.txt

feedback.correct:
while read line; do ... done < file.txt is the correct pattern.

Option A: $(cat) splits on spaces and newlines.
Option C: invalid syntax.
Option D: invalid syntax for read.

incorrect.A: $(cat) does not preserve lines intact

questions.question_text:
```bash
awk 'NF == 8 && $7 == 404' access.log | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
```
For the eight-field synthetic log format in sprint F3 (status field 7), what does this pipeline do?

options.text: Displays the first 5 lines with 404 errors
Displays top 5 IPs with the most 404 errors
Sorts the file and displays the first 5 lines

feedback.correct:
Step by step:
1. awk reads access.log
2. NF == 8 && $7 == 404 selects exactly eight-field rows whose status is 404
3. cut -d' ' -f1: extracts the first field (IP)
4. sort: sorts IPs (required for uniq)
5. uniq -c: counts occurrences
6. sort -rn: sorts numerically descending
7. head -5: first 5 results

Result: Top 5 IPs with the most 404 errors

incorrect.A: Does not understand that uniq -c counts
incorrect.C: Does not follow the entire pipeline

questions.question_text: Which command is equivalent to `cat file.txt | grep pattern`?

feedback.correct:
grep pattern file.txt is the direct form, without useless cat (UUOC).
grep accepts the file as an argument, does not require pipe from cat.
This is the recommended form for efficiency.

incorrect.B: Argument order for grep: pattern THEN file
incorrect.D: You cannot pipe a file name

questions.question_text: How do you run a command in background and make it immune to terminal closure?

feedback.correct:
nohup cmd & makes the command immune to SIGHUP (hangup signal on terminal closure).

cmd & only sends to background, but the process dies on terminal closure.
bg moves an ALREADY suspended job to background.
daemon is not a standard command.

incorrect.A: & alone does not protect from SIGHUP
incorrect.C: bg is for suspended jobs, not for launching
incorrect.D: daemon does not exist as a standard command

questions.question_text: What does the special variable $? contain in Bash?

options.text: The PID of the current process
The exit code of the last command executed

feedback.correct:
$? contains the exit code of the last command.
$$ = PID of the current process
$# = number of arguments
$0 = script name

incorrect.A: $$ is for PID

questions.question_text:
A colleague wrote:
```bash
for f in $(find . -name "*.log"); do
    rm "$f"
done
```
After reviewing the matching regular files in an owned exercise directory, which command performs the recursive deletion without splitting filenames?

options.text: The code is correct and safe

feedback.correct:
The keyed find command preserves filename boundaries and limits selection to regular files:
- Correctly handles spaces and special characters in names
- No separate rm process is needed for each file
- The live filesystem may change during traversal; preview is not an atomic snapshot

The colleague's code: problems with spaces in file names.
rm *.log: not recursive, may fail with "argument list too long".
ls | xargs rm: problems with spaces and special characters.

incorrect.A: $(find) causes problems with spaces in names
incorrect.C: rm *.log is not recursive and has limits
incorrect.D: ls | xargs rm has problems with special characters

questions.question_text:
An LLM generated this backup script:
```bash
#!/bin/bash
for f in *; do
    cp $f backup_$f
done
echo "Done"
```
What is the MOST CRITICAL problem with this code?

options.text: Unquoted variable $f fails for filenames with spaces
No error checking for cp command

feedback.correct:
The most critical problem is the unquoted variable $f.
When filenames contain spaces, $f without quotes causes word splitting.
Example: "my file.txt" becomes two arguments: "my" and "file.txt".

Correct: cp "$f" "backup_$f"

The shebang IS present (#!/bin/bash).
Missing error checking is important but less critical than broken functionality.
Comments are good practice but don't affect functionality.

incorrect.A: The shebang IS present in the code
incorrect.C: Error checking is important but less critical than broken core functionality

feedback.excellent: Congratulations! You have excellent mastery of shell scripting concepts.
feedback.good: Good level! Review pipes and subshells for improvement.
feedback.satisfactory: Good progress! Practise more with redirection and loops.
feedback.insufficient: Additional study required. Review the material and practise.
